summary: This standards-track document defines a TLV for IS-IS that records which router generated a purge. Purges currently carry no such information, so it is hard to find the source of problems. Because flooding does not change the purge contents, the TLV remains attached as the purge spreads.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6232 adds a Purge Originator Identification field to IS-IS purge messages. Routers can use it to record who created the purge and, when necessary, which neighbor passed it along.

questions: how to find which router purged an is-is lsp
what is the is-is purge originator identification tlv
how do i find which router sent an is-is purge
subtitle: An IS-IS field that records which router created a purge and can identify the neighbor that passed it on.

tldr.problem: IS-IS purges are flooded without identifying the system that created them, making unexpected purges difficult to trace.
tldr.mechanism: The Purge Originator Identification TLV carries the inserting system's ID and may also carry the ID of the neighbor from which the purge arrived; a Dynamic Hostname TLV may add a readable name.
tldr.outcome: Operators can identify the origin or upstream source of a purge. RFC 6232 updates RFCs 5301, 5304 and 5310, and was updated by RFC 8918.

today: RFC 6232 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2011. It updates RFC 5301, RFC 5304 and RFC 5310, and has been updated by RFC 8918.

sections.title: Why Purges Need an Origin
sections.content:
IS-IS floods a purge through an area regardless of which Intermediate System (IS) started it. A purge tells other routers to remove an old link-state protocol data unit. Without origin information, an operator investigating an unexpected purge has difficulty locating the source.

RFC 6232 defines a Type-Length-Value (TLV) that records the system ID of the IS that generates the purge. The RFC notes that implementations have sometimes generated purges improperly, including after receiving a corrupted link-state packet.
sections.plainLanguage: A purge tells routers to remove old routing information, but older purges did not identify their source. This RFC adds a field that records the system that created one.

sections.title: The Purge Originator TLV
sections.content:
The Purge Originator Identification (POI) TLV uses code 13. Its value begins with a one-octet count of the system IDs that follow. The defined counts are 1 or 2: the first ID names the IS that inserted the TLV, and the optional second ID names the IS from which the purge was received.

The POI TLV should appear in all purges. It must not appear in an LSP whose Remaining Lifetime is non-zero, so it is limited to purge messages.
sections.plainLanguage: The field records one router ID, or two when it also records the neighbor that passed the purge on. It belongs on purges, not on active link-state messages.

sections.title: Adding and Propagating the Origin
sections.content:
An IS that generates a purge should add the POI TLV with its own system ID. If an IS receives a purge without the TLV, it should add its own system ID and the ID of the neighbor that sent it.

Normal LSP flooding does not change the message contents, so the identifying information travels with the purge. A receiving router can log the originator or the upstream source to help locate the cause.
sections.plainLanguage: The router that creates a purge records its own ID. If a router receives an unmarked purge, it records itself and the neighbor that sent it.

sections.title: Adding a Dynamic Hostname
sections.content:
The RFC extends use of the Dynamic Hostname TLV, type 137, so it may also appear in purges. Implementations should include one instance when they include the POI TLV. Only the local hostname should be inserted.

A hostname gives operators a human-readable way to identify a system alongside its system ID.
sections.plainLanguage: A router may include its hostname with the system ID. The hostname is easier for an operator to recognize.

sections.title: Authentication and Network Readiness
sections.content:
With authentication from RFC 5304 or RFC 5310, legacy systems that strictly follow those RFCs will discard purges carrying these extensions. That could make routing databases inconsistent if only some routers support the change.

In an authenticated domain, every implementation must be upgraded to receive the POI TLV before any IS is allowed to generate a purge that contains it. RFC 6232 points to RFC 6233 for further interactions among the POI, Dynamic Hostname and Authentication TLVs.
sections.plainLanguage: Older authenticated routers may discard a purge that contains the new field. All routers in the domain must be ready to receive it before any router sends one.

sections.title: The Assigned TLV Code
sections.content: IANA assigned code point 13 to the Purge Originator Identification TLV in the IS-IS TLV Codepoints registry. The TLV is allowed in LSPs and purges, but not in IS-IS Hello PDUs or Sequence Number PDUs.
sections.plainLanguage: The POI TLV has the shared code number 13. The RFC also specifies which IS-IS message types may carry it.
